opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I look back, I think there's actually been one consistent question running through all of it, which is how we get machines to really understand and use language, not just as a pattern-matching exercise, but as a way of getting things done in the world.

During my PhD at MIT, I started out in NLP, and at the time I was struck by how much of language understanding was being treated as a static, supervised problem. You'd have a sentence, you'd have a label, and you'd train a model to predict it. But that's not how people learn language. We learn it by interacting, by acting and seeing what happens. So I became really interested in bringing reinforcement learning together with language. Some of my early work was on teaching agents to play text-based games, where the agent had to read a description of the world, decide what to do, and learn from the outcome. Language wasn't just the input to be classified. It was tied to meaning through action.

Then I went to OpenAI, and that's where I worked with Alec Radford and others on what became the first GPT paper. That took me in a somewhat different direction, focused on the power of generative pre-training. The idea was that you could learn a tremendous amount about language just by modeling text at scale and then transfer that to downstream tasks. Even then, we were surprised at how well it worked, and the later scaling really exceeded what many of us expected.

When I came to Princeton, those two threads started to come back together. Once you have these very capable language models, the natural question is: what can they do beyond producing a good response? Can they reason, make plans, use tools, interact with environments, and accomplish a task over multiple steps? That's where language agents come in. With work like ReAct, for instance, along with my students and collaborators, we explored how interleaving reasoning with actions lets a model take on tasks that it couldn't handle otherwise.

So in a way, it feels like coming full circle. The early RL work had the right framing, with agents acting in the world through language, but the models weren't yet powerful enough. Generative models supplied that missing capability. Now we can combine them, and I think the big open questions are about making these agents reliable, measuring how well they do on real tasks, and getting them to the point where people can actually trust them with meaningful work.

r001.rationale: The response argues that language should be connected to acting in and accomplishing tasks in the world, rather than treated as an isolated pattern-matching or prediction problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, when I look back, it feels more coherent in hindsight than it did while I was living it. But there is a thread, and the thread is this question of how an agent can use language to act in the world and learn from it.

My PhD at MIT was actually about exactly that, before it was fashionable. I was working on things like learning to play text-based games with reinforcement learning, and on using text instructions to guide an agent, for example reading a game manual to play Civilization better. The core idea was that language isn't just something you process and classify. It carries knowledge about how the world works, and an agent should be able to read that knowledge and use it to make better decisions. At the time, the models were tiny, the environments were toy, and most of the field saw RL and NLP as two separate communities that didn't talk much.

Then I spent time at OpenAI, and that's where the GPT work happened. What was striking about that was realizing that if you just scale up generative pretraining on text, you get a model that absorbs an enormous amount of that world knowledge for free. That changed what was possible. The "reading a manual" problem suddenly looked very different, because the model has already read most of the manuals.

So when I came to Princeton, the natural question became: now that we have these powerful language models, can we go back to the original dream and actually build agents out of them? That led to things like ReAct, where the model interleaves reasoning and acting, Tree of Thoughts for more deliberate search, and then benchmarks like WebShop and SWE-bench, because we needed realistic environments to measure whether these agents actually work.

So I'd describe the trajectory as: I started with the agent question when the tools weren't ready, took a detour to help build the tools, and then came back to the question. The RL side gave me the vocabulary of actions, environments, and feedback. The NLP side gave the models. Language agents are where those two finally meet, and I think we're still very early in figuring out what that looks like.

r001.rationale: The response argues that language carries knowledge about how the world works and should guide an agent’s actions and learning, connecting language processing to its broader context in the world.

astra-6.text:
For me, the connecting thread is how language can help an AI system make decisions and act. NLP gives you a way to understand and represent information, while reinforcement learning asks how you use that information to choose actions and learn from their consequences.

Language agents bring those questions together. Instead of a model just producing an answer, it can use language to interpret a goal, decide what to do, interact with an environment, and respond to feedback. That also changes what we need to evaluate: producing something plausible is different from actually accomplishing a task.

So I see it as a fairly continuous trajectory. The models and their capabilities have changed, but the underlying question remains: how do we connect language understanding with useful behavior?

r001.rationale: The response connects language understanding to goals, actions, environmental interaction, and feedback, arguing that language should be considered in the context of behavior rather than in isolation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the connecting thread has been learning how to use language to make decisions. In NLP, we often focus on understanding or generating text, and in reinforcement learning, we focus on an agent taking actions and learning from the consequences. What interested me was the intersection: how can language help an agent understand its environment, acquire knowledge, and decide what to do next?

Language is a really useful interface for that. You can describe a goal, give instructions, or communicate something that would otherwise take an agent many interactions to discover. And the relationship goes both ways: interacting with an environment gives language a purpose and a way to test whether the system actually understood something.

So I see language agents as a natural continuation of those interests. Once you have a model that can work with language, the next question is how to connect it to actions and feedback. Can it make a plan, carry it out, recognize when something went wrong, and adjust? That brings together the language side and the sequential decision-making side in a very direct way.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames language as connected to agents’ environments, actions, consequences, and feedback, arguing that interaction gives language purpose and tests understanding.
